subject: Performance SLO follow-up: latency/throughput targets & cost levers
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Samir Gupta <samir@novaretail.com>, Olivia Chen <olivia.chen@novaretail.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 06 May 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Performance SLO follow-up: latency/throughput targets & cost levers

Thanks again for the time today — really helpful to see the demo flow and the traffic shape you expect for the contextual recommendations feature. Quick recap + next steps so we don't lose momentum.

Recap (what we heard)
- Primary SLO: p95 latency target for end-to-end response (app-level): goal is 250-300ms for short answers (<=64 output tokens). Streaming required for longer, multi-chunk responses (recommendation text).
- Expected steady-state throughput: ~200 concurrent active users during normal hours; peak burst up to ~500 concurrent during promotional events.
- Typical request size: short prompts (20-40 input tokens), average outputs ~120 tokens when full recommendation is returned.
- Availability: multi-region failover desirable, start with us region.

Open items we flagged on the call
- Confirm p95 target you want to commit to for peak events vs normal traffic (250ms vs 300ms).
- Confirm whether strict streaming on every request is required or only for responses >128 tokens.
- Provide a short sample of production traces (1-2 hrs) or a synthetic QPS profile so we can run an accurate perf run.

Cost / performance levers we discussed
- Continuous batching: reduces per-token compute by aggregating requests; tunable by latency budget.
- KV/prefix caching: cache common prefixes/context to avoid repeated decoding work for chat-like flows.
- Quantization profiles: 8-bit/4-bit quantized variants give big cost reductions at modest quality tradeoffs (we can A/B).
- Model variants: smaller quantized models (redwood-3b-quant) for high-concurrency low-latency paths; larger models for higher-quality offline/async flows.
- Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs: streaming reduces perceived latency for the user, but can increase server-side tail if not implemented with early-decode kernels — we can tune batching windows to mitigate.

Proposed next steps
1) Please confirm p95 target (250ms or 300ms) and whether streaming required for all requests.
2) Share a 1-2 hour sample of your traffic profile (or simple QPS + token distribution) — we can use this to run a 48-hour perf test.
3) Rishi to run a technical deep-dive on perf knobs and a perf-test plan (I attached a short proposal and the call recording).

Attachments: redwood-performance-slo-proposal.pdf, demo-recording-20260506.mp4

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick follow-up if you want to walk through the proposal.

—

Subject: Re: Performance SLO follow-up: latency/throughput targets & cost levers

Appreciate the recap, Marissa — this matches our notes. A few clarifications from our side:
- We're comfortable with p95 = 300ms as a starting target for normal traffic, but during promotional/peak events we want p95 <= 350ms. Ultimately we'd like to tighten to 250-300ms after tuning.
- Streaming: we need streaming for any response that will be >128 tokens. For the short inline answers (<64 tokens) non-streamed is fine as long as p95 stays under the target.
- Concurrency: normal 200 concurrent, peak 500 — correct. We'll likely have short bursts that hit 700+ for 30-60s during flash events (we can simulate those in the perf test).
- Typical token counts: inputs 20-40 tokens, outputs 80-160 (mean ~120).

Questions:
1) How aggressive should we be with quantization for a first pass? Is 4-bit safe for our recommendation quality, or should we start with 8-bit and A/B?
2) How do you validate the SLO under streaming? Is the p95 measured on the last token end-to-end? We need that to be comparable to our client-side metrics.
3) Ballpark cost difference: hosted API vs dedicated reserved capacity — any rough numbers so we can budget?

We'll share a sample trace dump and a simple QPS distribution later today. Also, include any perf-test scripts + the perf plan in the next email and we'll get this scheduled.

Thanks,
Samir
Director of Engineering, Nova Retail
samir@novaretail.com

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.com>
To: Samir Gupta <samir@novaretail.com>, Olivia Chen <olivia.chen@novaretail.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 07 May 2026 10:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO follow-up: latency/throughput targets & cost levers

Thanks for the details, Samir — good set of questions. I pulled together a practical approach below that we can use for the perf run and initial config.

Measurement notes
- We measure p95 end-to-end at the API gateway (time from request arrival to final token commit). For streaming flows we provide stream-first latency (time to first byte) + final-completion p95. We can emit both so you can compare to client-side metrics.

Suggested perf/test configuration (to meet p95 ~300ms normal, 350ms peak)
- Routing: Route short requests to a "low-latency" pool running redwood-3b-quant (4-bit candidate) with aggressive early-decode kernels.
- Streaming: enable streaming for responses >128 tokens; tune batch window to 10-20ms to avoid adding tail latency for short requests.
- Batching: continuous batching with dynamic batch sizing; max batch window 20ms during normal traffic, increase to 40ms during peaks with higher concurrency.
- Caching: KV/prefix caching for repeated product-context prefixes — expect up to 15-25% token savings for common flows.
- Autoscaling: horizontal scaling with warm pool for peak protection; configure burst capacity to handle 2-3x baseline for 60-90s spikes.

Quantization and model variants
- Start with 8-bit quantized 3B for baseline A/B. If quality remains high on your eval prompts, trial 4-bit in a canary pool for traffic that tolerates small regressions.
- Keep a non-quantized 7B/13B model for fallback on high-accuracy paths (async/queued).

Ballpark cost levers (very rough estimates for planning)
- Hosted API (metered): easier to try, higher per-token cost but no infra commit. Good for piloting.
- Dedicated reserved capacity: lower per-token net cost at scale; breakeven depends on sustained volume (~hundreds of millions of tokens/mo).
- Quantization + continuous batching + caching typically reduce token-compute cost by ~30-60% depending on workload shape.

Immediate next steps I can run this week
1) I'll spin up a 48-hour perf test using your sample trace. I need the trace + expected user-concurrency windows (normal, peak, flash).
2) We'll run two model configs: redwood-3b-8bit (baseline) and redwood-3b-4bit (canary) with streaming enabled for >128 tokens.
3) We'll share a perf report with p50/p95/p99, cost projection, and suggested config for Dedicated vs Hosted.

I'll attach a short perf-test plan (perf-test-plan.md) and the run template in the Redwood Console. If that works I'll schedule the test for Friday.

—
Rishi Malhotra
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
rishi@redwood.com
